content.content:
929 agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md
5:JusPrin has one tool system with multiple adapters. New capabilities are added to the shared registry, executed by `ToolExecutionCoordinator`, and implemented through the typed live-workspace boundary; the OpenAI and MCP adapters only translate that contract to their wire formats. This guide keeps the catalog small, honest, safe to evolve, and driven by real printing tasks rather than an abstract feature inventory.
11:For local external clients, use the bundled `jusprin-mcp` stdio helper through **Connect AI tools...**. The helper and native server compile the same registry. Every new exposed tool must therefore have consistent live and offline catalog/schema behavior for the same build and negotiated protocol version; no new adapter-specific catalog is allowed. Direct HTTP is a developer route, not the default setup instruction.
83:Prefer typed reads with fixed schemas over one polymorphic record search. Sections of `workspace_inspect` each keep their own fixed shape; a generic `records_search` whose result shape depends on a `kind` argument makes the model guess.
87:Tool count is bounded by what a turn loads, not by what the app can do. The evidence behind these rules: OpenAI's function-calling guidance keeps fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn and defers the rest; Anthropic's [tool-writing guidance](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) asks for a few tools targeting high-impact workflows and names "tools that merely wrap existing software functionality or API endpoints" as the common error; a [domain-oriented MCP study](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.22063v1) measured a generic thin-tool interface below raw SQL and domain-shaped tools far above both; and the "god tool" that dispatches many unrelated actions through one `action` parameter is a documented anti-pattern. The current five-tool MCP catalog measures about 1.9 KB per definition, two thirds of it output schema.
95:- **The printer panel's session is the exception to "every tool loads".** Home's printer panel runs its own conversation with exactly one tool per mode: `printer_identify` when adding a printer, `printer_change` when changing one (`PrinterConversation::session_tools`). The app decides the tools; the words are the page's (`AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts` for the instructions, `AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts` for the notes the model reads after a tap), and a turn the page has not yet written them for is refused rather than sent with the project assistant's prompt. A Change session that could also identify a printer could clear the card of the printer it is about. Measured 2026-09-18 on the app's own request bodies against `gpt-5.4-mini`: Add sends one definition of 597 bytes and instructions of 28,425 bytes (the rules plus the 383-line printer list), about 11,540 input tokens per request, of which 11,008 came back cached on every request after the first of the day; the cold first request cached nothing. Change sends one definition of 832 bytes and about 552 input tokens, below the size OpenAI caches at all. Neither session carries the project: no workspace in the turn, none in a tool result.
97:- **Shape each tool as a domain operation.** A tool does one thing a slicer user would name: place an object, lay out the plates, mark a region, set up the printer. Not a wrapper per Orca function, and not an interpreter for a list of unrelated commands. Optional facets of one operation are fine when each is independently typed and conflicting facets are rejected.
100:- **Let call logs decide consolidation.** Two tools that transcripts show always called together are candidates to merge; two facets never used together are candidates to split. Consolidation follows evidence from evals, not the whiteboard.
101:- **Output schemas are not advertised over MCP.** No client was shown to use them, and they were two thirds of the catalog. `tools/list` stopped carrying `outputSchema`; `validate_output` still checks every MCP success, so a result that violates its contract still fails loudly. Measured on the same build with the recipe below: five tools, 9,723 bytes before, 3,141 after, about 2,430 tokens down to 785. The saving is MCP-side only: the in-app adapter has always sent `input_schema` as `parameters` and nothing else, so an in-app turn was never carrying them. Restore the field only for a client that is shown to read it.
105:Never put an enum value such as `printer | filament | process | object` in a schema unless every advertised value works in the fake and real adapter and has the documented inheritance behavior.
135:Do not let an adapter call `Plater`, `Model`, `PresetBundle`, wxWidgets, or slicing objects directly. Do not copy an Orca operation into JusPrin. When a required operation is trapped in presentation code, add the smallest behavior-oriented, product-neutral seam at its current owner.
143:- **Storage.** Project-scoped state (intent, plan, regions) lives in the 3mf auxiliary directory under `jusprin/`, using the same persistence, healing, and revert copy-forward the Agent bridge already uses for conversation state. In practice that means inside `state.json`, not beside it: `ProjectStateDocument` provisions a new top-level key on load without a schema bump, and the persistence tests assert that the JusPrin data directory holds exactly one file. The print intent (`printIntent`, upserted by field name, each with provenance), the plan (`plan`, replaced whole) and the region annotations (`regions`, replaced whole, each record stamped with a seq when it changes) are implemented there. Printer-scoped state (confirmed facts, monitoring policy) lives in app data keyed by printer identity, with `SpoolStore` as the precedent; confirmed facts carry an expiry because the physical world changes without telling the app. Regions and confirmed facts land with the tools that write them, since their record shapes are the geometry handles and printer identity those milestones define.
155:- strict input JSON Schema with `additionalProperties: false` where practical;
156:- output JSON Schema;
168:`ToolDefinition` currently stores name, title, description, input/output schemas, action class, exposure, availability and handler. Revision sensitivity, atomicity, cancellation and history semantics live in the coordinator/workspace implementation and tests, not in additional registry fields. `ToolAvailability` currently describes request context (`Always` or `ImportableAttachment`), not a dynamic project-state filter.
170:Input validation uses the registry's handler-specific `valid_arguments` decoder; changing only JSON Schema does not change accepted calls. MCP success output is checked by `validate_output`, whose schema vocabulary is deliberately limited. Extend that validator with tests before adding unsupported schema keywords. Do not assume it implements all of JSON Schema or that every adapter automatically validates output.
175:- Do not rename a released tool casually. Treat names and schemas as public APIs.
176:- Add optional fields compatibly. Do not change the meaning or type of an existing field.
187:- For a new read-modify-write operation that must detect changes since the caller's earlier read, design and test explicit expected-session/revision inputs in its own schema and decoder. Proposal-time checks alone do not prove the caller's earlier read is current; do not retrofit required arguments onto existing tools silently.
193:- Do not encode a large catalog as a schema enum; use bounded search and detail retrieval.
194:- **One exception, with its evidence: the printer list.** Identifying a printer from what someone says is the model's understanding, not a lookup, and a search tool in front of it did it badly: `printer_catalog_search` required every word of the query in a model's name and returned the first few in file order, so "voron 2.4 350mm" came back unsupported, "x1c" matched another manufacturer's printer and "prusa" showed three of thirteen. The Add session's instructions instead carry every printer the panel offers, one line each (`<catalogId> | <brand> <model> | <build volume>`, 383 lines from `PrinterCatalog::panel_printers`, sent to the page as the session's `context` and written into the instructions by `AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts`), and `printer_identify` checks the ids the model copies from it. Measured 2026-09-18 through the app's own request and tool results on `gpt-5.4-mini`, three runs of each case: the word test set 138/150, the photo test set 29/45, the handoff's own cases (those four queries among them) 21/21. The model tried to show more than three printers 33 times; each was refused with `too_many` and it then asked a narrowing question, so no answer ever showed three of many. The weak spots are a query that equals one model name and begins others ("bambu a1": 0/3) and photos with no readable name. The test sets and the runner are in `agent-docs/jusprin/spikes/printer-identify/` (uncommitted, beside the earlier spikes). The list is a fixed prefix of the instructions, so it caches; it is the right shape only while it stays a few hundred lines.
211:For new live-state contracts, include `sessionId` and `revision` when needed to identify and validate later calls. `workspace_inspect` returns both, with the selection as ids. Internal history-record results have their own schemas. MCP activity results also carry action ID, current session and revision in `_meta["io.jusprin/activity"]`. If an event says state changed, fetch a fresh snapshot; never treat the event itself as the new state.
213:For MCP success, produce schema-valid `structuredContent` and a serialized text block describing the same result. Errors use the shared `{error: {code, message, details}}` envelope with `isError: true`, not the success output schema. The bridge removes modern-only result/cache fields for legacy clients. For `2025-03-26` it also omits `structuredContent` and catalog `outputSchema`/`title`, preserving the serialized text result; later supported revisions retain `structuredContent` and `title`. No negotiated version advertises `outputSchema` any more (see [tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)); the bridge's own stripping stays because it also projects catalogs forwarded from a live app of another version. These are intentional compatibility projections, not conflicting tool definitions.
233:- invalid enum: key, diagnostic message, and valid values in `allowed`;
260:As implemented: `ToolDefinition::computation_only` feeds `approval_required(action_class, computation_only)`, and a destructive action never qualifies whatever it declares. Three places had treated "requires approval" as a synonym for "is a mutation" and now ask the action class directly — the coordinator's execution-time staleness recheck (an exempt mutation skips the card, not staleness, and is never `Pending` long enough for the eager invalidation to catch it), the MCP server's streaming decision, and the runtime's progress notifications, which say "Starting in JusPrin" where an approval-gated call says "Awaiting approval in JusPrin". No shipped tool declares the exemption yet and a test pins that; the coordinator's no-card tests arrive with `slice_start`, `plan_set`, and `activity_cancel`, because a test cannot supply its own catalog — the registry's constructor is private and its definitions are `const`.
264:A plan is several operations, and the user should review it once. Every mutation accepts an optional `planId`. Proposals sharing a `planId` render as one approval card that lists each operation, its class, and the plan headline from `plan_set`; the user approves or rejects the group. The group's class is the highest class of any member, and the card names the member that made it destructive. Each member is still validated, staleness-checked, and executed as its own proposal in order, so MCP tool annotations stay truthful per tool and a member that fails stale stops the rest. Grouping is a coordinator feature; it is never a reason to build one tool that takes a list of unrelated commands.
278:MCP progress notifications are optional request-scoped presentation. They must be monotonic and must not be the only way to learn the terminal result. Add the MCP Tasks extension only when a real client/eval needs durable calls that outlive one request; do not add it merely because an operation takes several seconds.
287:- attachment-based import (`object_import`) is in-app-only, and path-based `object_import_file` is MCP-only, because a file reaches the app through the conversation in one case and through an approved path in the other; that is two honest definitions over one workspace command, not one tool with forked behavior; and
295:Do not make MCP resources load-bearing until intended clients prove that model-driven resource retrieval is reliable. A bounded data-returning tool is the compatibility baseline. Resources may be added as an optional alternate projection of large, readable, stable data.
299:## Required implementation sequence for one new tool
307:7. Add the registry definition, decoder/validator, executor association, and output schema.
322:| Registry | unique name, deterministic ordering, valid schemas, correct exposure and action class |
327:| OpenAI adapter | canonical schema projection and successful continuation |
328:| MCP adapter | canonical schema/output projection, bounded response, protocol errors, disconnect behavior |
340:| `export_file` | Write the G-code or another file where the user wants it | destructive | both | a sliced plate, the project, placed objects or the presets in use; a path only as an approved input | the plate's G-code output, `Plater::export_3mf` with `Silence`, raw part meshes, `PresetBundle::export_current_configs` | 32 files, bytes, license and whether it restricts use, and for G-code and sliced 3MF up to 8 of the slice's own warnings (also on the card) |
344:| `object_divide` | Cut or split an object for printing | mutation | both | one object; one undo step | `Plater::apply_cut_object_to_model` after Orca's `Cut`, `Plater::split_object`, `ModelVolume::split` | 64 pieces as they now lie, overhang area before and after, 32 `regionsUnbound` |
345:| `object_divide_preview` | See the pieces before cutting | read-only | both | one object in a scratch model | `Cut`, `ModelObject::split` / `ModelVolume::split` on a copy | 64 pieces as they would lie, overhang area before and after (an estimate, not a slice), 32 regions that would unbind |
346:| `object_import` | Add the model the user attached | mutation | in-app | current document; importable attachment required | `IWorkspace::import_objects` over `Plater::load_files` with `ScopedModalAnswers` | new object ids and the questions answered |
349:| `object_place` | Stand, size and place an object for printing | mutation | both | one instance; one undo step | `Selection` transforms and the canvas `do_*` commits, `Plater::convert_unit`, `OrientJob` under a reporting wrapper | transform, size, optional job handle |
352:| `plate_layout` | Set copies, what prints, which plate, names and filaments, add and name plates, and arrange | mutation | both | objects and plates in one undo step; arrange as a job | `Plater::increase_instances`/`decrease_instances`, the object list's printable toggle, `Selection` moves, `PartPlateList::create_plate`, `PartPlate::set_bed_type`, `ArrangeJob` | the objects section, added plate ids, optional job handle |
377:`workspace_inspect` takes an optional `sections` list — `summary` (the default, and exactly what it returned before sections existed), `project`, `objects`, `intent`, `plan`, `slicing`, `history`, `printer`. The `objects` section lists every object (64, then `truncated`) with its plates, instance/part/modifier counts, printable flag, extruder, size and override count, from a separate adapter call so the snapshot every selection change builds stays cheap; it has no cursor yet. The `slicing` section also carries `jobs`: each Orca UI job a tool started (orient, arrange), with its handle, state, and for arrange the objects no plate holds afterwards. The `project` section reports the file's path, saved and preset-edit state, the file's own title, designer, description, license, copyright and origin (each `{value, provenance: "project_file"}`, present only when the file states it), the packed attachments by id (a read-only walk of the auxiliary folder without `JusPrin/` and `.thumbnails`; `ProjectPanel::Reload` would create folders), and whether an automatic backup covers the latest edits. The `printer` section sets the configured side (preset, model id, nozzles, plate, filament materials) beside the selected machine, with the facts the person confirmed under `factKey` (`device:<id>` when a machine is selected, otherwise `preset:<name>`) and computed `mismatches` for model, nozzle, filament material, and plate. No printer Orca talks to reports its plate, so `plateObservable` is false and a plate mismatch can only come from a confirmed fact. The `history` section extends the summary's `history` object with `restorable` and the steps, newest 32. Its output schema requires only the identity fields, so a caller that asks for one section is not handed the rest. It is no longer a strict OpenAI function: strict mode cannot express an optional argument.
420:**Reshaping (M5).** `object_divide_preview` runs Orca's `Cut` (which works on its own copy of the object) or `ModelObject::split` / `ModelVolume::split` on an object in a scratch `Model`; the harness proves the revision, the undo history and the dirty flag do not move. The preview reports pieces as they would lie and an overhang area (downward faces steeper than the process's support threshold, excluding the bed face): an estimate, not a slice. It does not return an image yet; that lands with the image projection in M6. `object_divide` follows `GLGizmoCut3D::perform_cut` without connectors (snapshot "Cut by Plane", `InvalidateCutInfo`, `Plater::apply_cut_object_to_model`), refuses an object already cut with connectors, and splits to objects through `Plater::split_object(false)` on the selected object (the index overload is declared upstream and never defined; auto-drop off avoids its only question), or to parts through `ModelVolume::split` as `ObjectList::split` does. `object_merge` selects exactly the named objects in the object list and runs its assemble, which takes its own snapshot. `object_repair` runs the repair command's per-part CGAL step without its progress dialog, clears the object's paint as Orca does when it does not remap it, and changes nothing when no part has open edges. `enum_bitmask`'s `|=` does not compile for `ModelObjectCutAttributes` (it assigns a bitmask to an int); combine with `|`.

5:JusPrin has one tool system with multiple adapters. New capabilities are added to the shared registry, executed by `ToolExecutionCoordinator`, and implemented through the typed live-workspace boundary; the OpenAI and MCP adapters only translate that contract to their wire formats. This guide keeps the catalog small, honest, safe to evolve, and driven by real printing tasks rather than an abstract feature inventory.
11:For local external clients, use the bundled `jusprin-mcp` stdio helper through **Connect AI tools...**. The helper and native server compile the same registry. Every new exposed tool must therefore have consistent live and offline catalog/schema behavior for the same build and negotiated protocol version; no new adapter-specific catalog is allowed. Direct HTTP is a developer route, not the default setup instruction.
83:Prefer typed reads with fixed schemas over one polymorphic record search. Sections of `workspace_inspect` each keep their own fixed shape; a generic `records_search` whose result shape depends on a `kind` argument makes the model guess.
87:Tool count is bounded by what a turn loads, not by what the app can do. The evidence behind these rules: OpenAI's function-calling guidance keeps fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn and defers the rest; Anthropic's [tool-writing guidance](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) asks for a few tools targeting high-impact workflows and names "tools that merely wrap existing software functionality or API endpoints" as the common error; a [domain-oriented MCP study](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.22063v1) measured a generic thin-tool interface below raw SQL and domain-shaped tools far above both; and the "god tool" that dispatches many unrelated actions through one `action` parameter is a documented anti-pattern. The current five-tool MCP catalog measures about 1.9 KB per definition, two thirds of it output schema.
95:- **The printer panel's session is the exception to "every tool loads".** Home's printer panel runs its own conversation with exactly one tool per mode: `printer_identify` when adding a printer, `printer_change` when changing one (`PrinterConversation::session_tools`). The app decides the tools; the words are the page's (`AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts` for the instructions, `AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts` for the notes the model reads after a tap), and a turn the page has not yet written them for is refused rather than sent with the project assistant's prompt. A Change session that could also identify a printer could clear the card of the printer it is about. Measured 2026-09-18 on the app's own request bodies against `gpt-5.4-mini`: Add sends one definition of 597 bytes and instructions of 28,425 bytes (the rules plus the 383-line printer list), about 11,540 input tokens per request, of which 11,008 came back cached on every request after the first of the day; the cold first request cached nothing. Change sends one definition of 832 bytes and about 552 input tokens, below the size OpenAI caches at all. Neither session carries the project: no workspace in the turn, none in a tool result.
97:- **Shape each tool as a domain operation.** A tool does one thing a slicer user would name: place an object, lay out the plates, mark a region, set up the printer. Not a wrapper per Orca function, and not an interpreter for a list of unrelated commands. Optional facets of one operation are fine when each is independently typed and conflicting facets are rejected.
100:- **Let call logs decide consolidation.** Two tools that transcripts show always called together are candidates to merge; two facets never used together are candidates to split. Consolidation follows evidence from evals, not the whiteboard.
101:- **Output schemas are not advertised over MCP.** No client was shown to use them, and they were two thirds of the catalog. `tools/list` stopped carrying `outputSchema`; `validate_output` still checks every MCP success, so a result that violates its contract still fails loudly. Measured on the same build with the recipe below: five tools, 9,723 bytes before, 3,141 after, about 2,430 tokens down to 785. The saving is MCP-side only: the in-app adapter has always sent `input_schema` as `parameters` and nothing else, so an in-app turn was never carrying them. Restore the field only for a client that is shown to read it.
105:Never put an enum value such as `printer | filament | process | object` in a schema unless every advertised value works in the fake and real adapter and has the documented inheritance behavior.
135:Do not let an adapter call `Plater`, `Model`, `PresetBundle`, wxWidgets, or slicing objects directly. Do not copy an Orca operation into JusPrin. When a required operation is trapped in presentation code, add the smallest behavior-oriented, product-neutral seam at its current owner.
143:- **Storage.** Project-scoped state (intent, plan, regions) lives in the 3mf auxiliary directory under `jusprin/`, using the same persistence, healing, and revert copy-forward the Agent bridge already uses for conversation state. In practice that means inside `state.json`, not beside it: `ProjectStateDocument` provisions a new top-level key on load without a schema bump, and the persistence tests assert that the JusPrin data directory holds exactly one file. The print intent (`printIntent`, upserted by field name, each with provenance), the plan (`plan`, replaced whole) and the region annotations (`regions`, replaced whole, each record stamped with a seq when it changes) are implemented there. Printer-scoped state (confirmed facts, monitoring policy) lives in app data keyed by printer identity, with `SpoolStore` as the precedent; confirmed facts carry an expiry because the physical world changes without telling the app. Regions and confirmed facts land with the tools that write them, since their record shapes are the geometry handles and printer identity those milestones define.

156:- output JSON Schema;

194:- **One exception, with its evidence: the printer list.** Identifying a printer from what someone says is the model's understanding, not a lookup, and a search tool in front of it did it badly: `printer_catalog_search` required every word of the query in a model's name and returned the first few in file order, so "voron 2.4 350mm" came back unsupported, "x1c" matched another manufacturer's printer and "prusa" showed three of thirteen. Measured 2026-09-18 through the app's own request and tool results on `gpt-5.4-mini`, three runs of each case: the word test set 138/150, the photo test set 29/45, the handoff's own cases (those four queries among them) 21/21. The model tried to show more than three printers 33 times; each was refused with `too_many` and it then asked a narrowing question, so no answer ever showed three of many. The weak spots are a query that equals one model name and begins others ("bambu a1": 0/3) and photos with no readable name. The test sets and the runner are in `agent-docs/jusprin/spikes/printer-identify/` (uncommitted, beside the earlier spikes). The list is a fixed prefix of the instructions, so it caches; it is the right shape only while it stays a few hundred lines.
211:For new live-state contracts, include `sessionId` and `revision` when needed to identify and validate later calls. `workspace_inspect` returns both, with the selection as ids. Internal history-record results have their own schemas. MCP activity results also carry action ID, current session and revision in `_meta["io.jusprin/activity"]`. If an event says state changed, fetch a fresh snapshot; never treat the event itself as the new state.
213:For MCP success, produce schema-valid `structuredContent` and a serialized text block describing the same result. Errors use the shared `{error: {code, message, details}}` envelope with `isError: true`, not the success output schema. The bridge removes modern-only result/cache fields for legacy clients. For `2025-03-26` it also omits `structuredContent` and catalog `outputSchema`/`title`, preserving the serialized text result; later supported revisions retain `structuredContent` and `title`. No negotiated version advertises `outputSchema` any more (see [tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)); the bridge's own stripping stays because it also projects catalogs forwarded from a live app of another version. These are intentional compatibility projections, not conflicting tool definitions.

260:As implemented: `ToolDefinition::computation_only` feeds `approval_required(action_class, computation_only)`, and a destructive action never qualifies whatever it declares. 440:**Grouped approvals (M7).** The registry adds an optional `planId` (1 to 64 characters) to every mutation's schema except `plan_set` (`joins_plans`), so those tools use non-strict function calling; `validate_call` checks it, refuses it on a read, keeps it away from the tool's own decoder and puts it back for the coordinator, which records it on the activity (saved in `state.json`, sent to the page as `planId`). A member always waits for approval, including a computation-only call that would otherwise run without a card. `plan_set` is left out because a live run read "make these changes as one plan" as a call to it with a `planId`, and grouping the agent's own words adds nothing to the card. Both adapters answer a member at once instead of waiting for the card, because the person can decide only after the agent has proposed the rest: the in-app agent gets `{"state":"queued", "planId", "actionId", "message"}` as its function output, and an MCP client gets the same text with no `structuredContent` (it is not the tool's result; `_meta["io.jusprin/activity"].state` is `queued`). The server advertises no `outputSchema`, so no client expects structured content from it. The outcome is read later from the new `activities` section of `workspace_inspect` (the latest 20 calls with state, plan and error). `approve` or `reject` on any member decides every waiting member; `pump` runs a plan's members in proposal order, one at a time, and holds a later member while an earlier one is still running (a slice that waits). Staleness for a member counts only changes from outside the plan: a change that arrives while another member of the same plan executes does not count, and any other content or settings change after approval fails the next member as `stale_revision`. Settings patches in a plan skip the revision half of their own guard for the same reason; the confirmed before-values still guard every key. A member that fails fails the plan's remaining approved members as `plan_step_failed`; members already done stay done. The page draws one card per plan beneath the message that proposed its first member (and in the external-tools area for MCP plans), titled with the latest `plan_set` headline, listing each member with its state, naming the member that makes the plan destructive, with one Approve all / Reject all that sends the decision for the first waiting member. While the in-app agent's turn is still streaming, those buttons are disabled ("The Agent is still adding to this plan"), so a person cannot approve half a plan. An MCP plan has no such signal; its card is live as soon as its first member arrives.

Checked against agent-docs/jusprin/mcp-tool-extension-guide.md. A typed call is what the guide wants, but not in the form I suggested.

What the guide says that applies:
- "strict input JSON Schema with additionalProperties: false where practical" (line 155), so tightening is in scope.
- "Shape each tool as a domain operation... Optional facets of one operation are fine when each is independently typed and conflicting facets are rejected" (line 97). Connect is one operation with two facets (a Bambu device, or a host address), so one tool is the preferred shape.
- "Input unions such as the facets of object_place are the decoder's job, not the schema validator's" (line 601), and "changing only JSON Schema does not change accepted calls" (line 170). So an anyOf in the schema is against the convention, and a schema change alone would not fix anything.
- Two tools are allowed by precedent (object_import vs object_import_file, line 287, "two honest definitions over one workspace command"), but that precedent exists because the file reaches the app by different routes, not because the model needed help. Not the case here.
- The OpenAI adapter deliberately uses non-strict function calling for tools with optional facets and leaves acceptance to native validation (line 473).

So the guide-shaped fix: keep one printer_connect, and make its valid_arguments branch in ToolRegistry.cpp (line ~611) require exactly one facet: deviceId alone, or hostType together with an address that matches a host, IP or URL shape, no spaces. Today that branch accepts any combination of the three. Say the same rule in the schema descriptions so the model reads it. Then preflight_tool keeps only the check no shape can express: an address the person never wrote is refused with address_needed.

The rename and "no retrofitted required arguments" rules (lines 175 and 187) do not bind here because the printer tools have not shipped to users.

I have rewritten finding 02's suggested change in the report to this.

Yes. PrinterConversation::preflight_tool exists in HEAD; it arrived with commit 7f66e75b07 (2026-09-18, "Let the model understand the printer, and the app do what it already knows"). PrinterPanel.cpp line 90 registers it with the coordinator through set_session_tool_preflight, and ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp line 763 calls it after the registry's valid_arguments check and before the approval card is drawn, so an error it returns goes back to the model as the tool result and no card appears.

Today it only acts on printer_connect: it refuses when no printer is saved yet or a connection is already being checked, resolves a Bambu device by id or name against the discovered list, and for a host requires that hostType and address are present. The card's title ("Connect to <address>") is also set there. What it lacks is any check of what the address is, which is why "Creality K1" got through and became a card.

So nothing new is needed structurally: the decoder change in ToolRegistry.cpp handles the shape, and the one extra rule (an address the person never wrote) is a few lines in the existing host branch of this function.

input.text:
Keep it enabled. But first a fact from the code that changes the question: today the two connect paths behave differently while connecting.

For Moonraker/OctoPrint the test is synchronous on the main thread. OrcaPrinterBackend::connect_host (line ~425) runs host->test() under a wxBusyCursor, so for those ~30 seconds the whole app is frozen: the composer is not "enabled", it is unreachable, and anything typed lands after the test returns. That is the real cause of the silence in finding 03, not only missing card copy. Moving that test off the main thread comes before any composer decision.

For Bambu the attempt is asynchronous: the conversation sets m_connecting, tick() polls, and the outcome arrives as a note plus a queued turn. The composer stays enabled, and that is the right design for both paths once the host test is asynchronous too.

What should happen if the person types during the wait:
- The message sends as normal and the model answers it. The prompt already tells the model that "connecting" means the app is waiting and to say so in one line, so a question like "how long does this take" gets a sane answer.
- The outcome keeps its place in the thread. AgentHost::start_turn queues the outcome turn behind any message the person already sent, so the reply to the person comes first, then "Connected" or "Couldn't reach it". Nothing is lost or reordered.
- A new address while connecting ("sorry, it's 192.168.1.43") is the one case to design. Today preflight refuses a second printer_connect with connection_in_progress, which sends the person back to waiting for an attempt they already know is wrong. Better: a new printer_connect cancels the running attempt and starts the new one, and the card for the old attempt reads "Cancelled". A Cancel button on the "Connecting…" card covers the same need without typing.
- What to avoid: disabling the composer with a "please wait" state. That is the form thinking the rebuild removed, and a locked input during a 30 second wait is exactly when people want to say something.

For Moonraker/OctoPrint the test is synchronous on the main thread. input.text:
Less than it sounds, and the two examples need different amounts.

"How long does this take" needs no tool. The wait is a fixed budget: OrcaPrinterBackend::connection reports the attempt as failed after 30 seconds (line 326). Put that number where the model can read it, in the printer_connect result ("connecting; the app gives it up to 30 seconds") and in the one prompt line that already explains "connecting". The model answers from context, and the thread already carries the question and answer in order. Cost: two strings.

"Sorry, it's 192.168.1.43" is the one that needs plumbing, and here is the whole list:
1. The host test off the main thread (already needed for finding 03; today it blocks everything, so nothing can be typed at all).
2. A cancel on the backend: something that ends a running attempt and marks it. Today there is none. For Bambu it is clearing m_connecting and the selection the attempt made; for a host it is dropping the test's result when it comes back.
3. preflight_tool lets a new printer_connect cancel the running attempt and proceed instead of returning connection_in_progress.
4. The coordinator marks the superseded activity cancelled so its card reads "Cancelled" (the reject path already produces that state for a pending card; this reuses it for a running one).
No new tool, no new schema, no new page message. The Cancel button on the "Connecting…" card rides on the same backend cancel through the existing tool_decision reject.

What the model does not need: a way to see progress mid-attempt. There is no progress to see; the attempt is a single test with a deadline, and its end arrives as a note that starts a turn. Anything typed in between is a normal message answered from the conversation the model already has.

So the honest sizing: the asynchronous host test is the real work, the cancel is small once that exists, and the rest is wiring.

input.text:
Finding 03 now says the tool-result message explicitly (the connect result's empty "message" becomes "The app is checking the printer now and gives it up to 30 seconds", copied from the backend's constant).

For the synchronous host test, my suggestion is to make the host path look like the Bambu path, which is already asynchronous, so the conversation layer needs no new machinery.

How the Bambu path works today: connect_printer records a ConnectionAttempt with a start time and returns at once; connect() answers the model with state "connecting"; OrcaPrinterBackend::connection() reads the attempt on every call and turns it into verified, failed, or connecting with a 30-second deadline (line ~326); PrinterConversation::tick() polls once a second, and when the state leaves "connecting" it posts the note and starts the turn.

The host change, in the backend only:
1. connect_host keeps its validation and configure_named_printer_host as they are, then instead of running host->test() inline it fills the existing HostAttempt with state "connecting" and a start time, plus an attempt number, and returns.
2. The test runs on a worker thread that owns the PrintHost (the unique_ptr moves into the thread; nothing in the thread touches the panel, the plater or the config). When test() returns, the thread writes {attempt number, passed, detail} into a shared result slot (a shared_ptr the backend and the thread both hold, guarded by a mutex or an atomic state). Detached, or joined in the destructor: curl tests end on their own timeout, so a join is bounded.
3. connection() reads the slot the way it reads the Bambu attempt: same attempt number → verified or failed with the test's message; still running past 30 seconds → failed with "did not respond"; otherwise connecting.
4. connect() in PrinterConversation returns "connecting" for a host too, and the existing tick() does the rest: the outcome note, the printers_changed, the turn.

What this buys beyond unblocking the UI: the cancel from earlier in this thread is an attempt number bump. A result arriving for an old number is dropped, so a superseded attempt, a panel that closed, or a printer renamed mid-test cannot write anywhere that matters. That is the concern in the current comment ("no background callback that can outlive the panel or target a new selection"), answered by ownership rather than by staying synchronous.

What it does not do: interrupt curl mid-request. It does not need to; the person is never waiting on the old attempt once its number is stale.

Size: one struct field, one thread, one branch in connection(), one line in connect(). PhysicalPrinterDialog keeps its own synchronous test; this does not touch upstream code.

No on both counts. The Bambu path's asynchronous part is ours, and the host change stays in our files too.

What is upstream on the Bambu path: the network agent, DeviceManager, and MachineObject, which keep talking to the printer in the background on their own threads and publish their state (last message times, selected machine). The fork does not modify them for this. What is ours: OrcaPrinterBackend (src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/PrinterSetup/, added in 0e55c4f9be) records the attempt with its start time and reads upstream's published state on every connection() call to decide connecting, verified, or failed. So the "async" is our polling of state upstream already keeps.

For Moonraker/OctoPrint there is no background state to poll, so we create the one thing missing, a worker thread that runs the test, and that thread lives in OrcaPrinterBackend as well. Everything it touches is either ours (NamedPrinters::configure_named_printer_host, the HostAttempt record) or upstream code called as a library without modification: PrintHost::get_print_host to build the adapter, and PrintHost::test, a const virtual with no UI dependency. Calling it off the main thread has upstream's own precedent: PrintHostJobQueue runs every upload on a bg_thread (PrintHost.cpp line 147), so the adapters already run on worker threads in the shipped app.

What we do not touch: PhysicalPrinterDialog keeps its synchronous test with the busy cursor; GUI_App, DeviceManager and PrintHost stay as they are. No new seam in an upstream file, nothing extra to carry through a rebase.

input.text:
You are right, that was sloppy wording. Let me separate the two things I collapsed into "asynchronous".

The background work on the Bambu path is upstream's. Upstream's network agent and DeviceManager talk to the printer on their own threads whether or not our panel exists. Nothing in the fork started that or changed it.

What is ours is the way our connect call avoids blocking: connect_printer returns immediately and connection() later reads the state upstream keeps. That is a non-blocking design in our backend, but it is not us doing background work. Calling it "the asynchronous part is ours" overstated it.

So the precise statement: for Bambu, upstream does the background work and we poll it; for Moonraker/OctoPrint, upstream offers only a blocking test call, so we have to supply the background work ourselves, with a worker thread in our backend that calls upstream's test as a library. The two paths then look the same from the conversation's side (an attempt with a start time, polled by connection(), reported by tick()), which is the only sense in which "make the host path look like the Bambu path" holds.

The conclusion about upstream files does not change: neither path needs an upstream edit. Upstream's Bambu code is used as is, and upstream's PrintHost::test is called as is, from a thread we own, the same way upstream's own upload queue already calls the adapters from its bg_thread.

Kenneth settled this on 2026-09-23. In the printer setup flow, "connect your printer" is user wording. For the code it means: find or enter the printer's connection details, check that they work, and save them with that printer. The check may open a real connection for a moment. Setup does NOT promise that the connection stays active after a later printer-profile change.

- After the connection software changes, printer status stays "connected" for up to 30 seconds. That is the normal freshness window in `has_recent_printer_data`, the same one that applies when a printer is switched off. It is not a regression.

Answers in order. Two of them are Kenneth's call and I say which.

1. Where the failure chips come from. Agree with the app attaching them, with one caveat: the handoff records Kenneth's decision that "the assistant decides which reply buttons to show" (decision 1). This is a departure for one case, so Kenneth should confirm it. My argument for it: the failure is an app event (the app already authors the note "Connection to X failed: ..."), and a chip row that must always appear cannot depend on a model that skipped an explicit rule in 6 of 10 runs. If Kenneth keeps decision 1, the fallback is to put the exact "Choices: Try again | Enter the details myself | Skip for now" line inside the app's failure note; models copy text far more reliably than they follow rules, and the harness can count it.

2. What the chips do. "Enter the details myself" → the model calls printer_manual_connection, which already exists and opens Orca's printer settings for this printer; the prompt already names it as the after-two-failures fallback (line 65). "Skip for now" ends the connect step only. The conversation stays open, the assistant says the printer is ready to slice and that Connect… on its Home card is there for later, and offers ( Done ). Only Done calls printer_setup_finish, which closes the panel; the prompt forbids calling it unasked (line 66), keep that.

3. What Cancel and failure leave behind. Fix it here, at least for the host path, because the thread makes it free: the worker owns its own copy of the config, so connect_host no longer needs to write the profile before testing. Write the address and key only on verified; Cancel and failure leave the profile as it was. That is finding 04 for hosts. For Bambu, link_named_printer and set_selected_machine happen before the result because upstream needs the selection to attempt; on failure or cancel, undo both (unlink, restore the previous selection). If that undo turns out larger than a few lines, keep it as separate work under finding 04 and say so in the PR. Kenneth's settled meaning of "connect" is "verify and save", which reads as: save what verified, not what was tried.

4. The detached thread. Acceptable, with two facts to design around. First, Http's DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MAX is 0 (Http.cpp line 104), so a listener that accepts and never answers holds test() open with no upper bound; only the connect timeout (10 s) is bounded. Our 30-second deadline reports failure, but the thread lives on. Second, CurlGlobalInit runs curl_global_cleanup from a static destructor at exit (Http.cpp line 81), so a detached thread still inside curl at exit is a possible exit-time crash, which would reach Sentry. So: detach, have the thread own everything (config copy, PrintHost, shared result slot tagged with the attempt number), drop late results, and accept the exit case but make it rare: the silent-listener case is the harness fixture, not a real network, and real failures resolve within the 10-second connect timeout. Do not join in the backend destructor; a join can stall panel close for as long as the server dawdles.

5. Testing plan. Keep all of it. Add: a Cancel from the card while connecting (reject on a running activity → "Cancelled", attempt dropped); the panel closing mid-test (no crash, late result dropped, nothing written); failure and cancel leave the profile unchanged (the finding 04 half); and in Vitest the "Cancelled" card state. The "show the bug first" measurement: a wx timer that should tick every 100 ms and does not while test() runs is a clean number.

Live run: a few runs looked over by hand are enough for the mechanics, because tool ordering, the queued outcome turn and the profile writes are app behaviour, not model behaviour, and the unit tests cover them. Use the measured 10-per-arm batch only if the chips stay prompt-driven (option 1's fallback), since then the thing under test is the model's compliance. Three hand-checked runs per path (host failure, host success against a local listener that answers /server/info, Bambu with the fake) is the right size.

"Chips" are the reply buttons: the pill-shaped suggested replies under an assistant message ("Yes, connect it", "No, thanks", the three Prusa names). Tapping one sends its text as the person's message. The handoff calls them reply buttons (section 4.2); the page's CSS class is reply-chip, which is the word I picked up. Same thing.

Why after a failure: in the live run the failed attempt ended with "I couldn't reach it at 192.168.1.42. Please check the address... then send it again", and nothing else. The person's next move is one of three known things (try the same address again, enter the details in Orca's own settings, or leave it for now), and the second of those is a path they cannot discover by typing. That was the "dead end" in finding 03.

Whether they need to be buttons is your call, and the honest answer is no. The requirement is only that the failure reply names the ways forward. input.text:
Full response to the coding agent's five questions, self-contained.

1. Where the ways forward after a failure come from. No reply buttons. The assistant's failure reply names the three options in words: try the same address again; enter the details in Orca's printer settings; or leave it for now, with the printer still ready to slice. The prompt (printerInstructions.ts, connect rules) states those three. The app attaches nothing to the failure beyond the note it already posts ("Connection to X failed: ..."). Because compliance here is the model's, this is the one place a measured batch is worth running: 10 live failure runs, count how many replies name all three.

2. What the person's answers do. "I'll enter the details myself" (any wording) → the model calls printer_manual_connection, which exists and opens Orca's printer settings for this printer; the prompt already names it as the fallback (line 65). "Skip for now" (any wording) ends the connect step only: the conversation stays open, the assistant says the printer is ready to slice and that Connect… on its Home card is there for later, and waits. Only the person's explicit Done leads to printer_setup_finish, which closes the panel; the prompt forbids calling it unasked (line 66). Keep that.

3. What Cancel and failure leave behind. Fix it in this change for the host path, because the worker thread makes it free: the thread owns its own copy of the config, so connect_host no longer needs to write the profile before testing. Write the address and API key to the profile only when the test passes; Cancel and failure leave the profile as it was. That is finding 04 for Moonraker/OctoPrint. For Bambu, link_named_printer and set_selected_machine run before the result because upstream needs the selection to attempt; on failure or cancel, undo both (unlink, restore the previous selection). If that undo is more than a few lines, keep it as separate work under finding 04 and say so in the PR. The settled meaning of "connect" is verify and save: save what verified, not what was tried.

4. The detached thread. Acceptable, with two facts to design around. Http's DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MAX is 0 (Http.cpp line 104), so a listener that accepts and never answers holds test() open with no upper bound; only the connect timeout (10 s) is bounded. Our 30-second deadline reports the failure, but the thread lives on. And CurlGlobalInit runs curl_global_cleanup from a static destructor at exit (Http.cpp line 81), so a detached thread still inside curl at exit is a possible exit-time crash, which would reach Sentry. So: detach; the thread owns everything it uses (config copy, PrintHost, a shared result slot tagged with the attempt number); a late result is dropped; do not join in the backend destructor, since a join can stall panel close for as long as the server dawdles. Accept the exit case: the never-answering listener is a test fixture, and real failures resolve inside the 10-second connect timeout.

5. Testing. Keep the plan as written. Add: a Cancel from the card while connecting (reject on a running activity → the card reads "Cancelled", the attempt number is bumped, the late result is dropped); the panel closing mid-test (no crash, nothing written, late result dropped); failure and cancel leave the profile unchanged (question 3); the "Cancelled" card state in Vitest; and the harness live check that a failure reply names the three ways forward (question 1). For "show the bug first", a wx timer that should tick every 100 ms and does not while test() runs is a clean measurement.

Live runs: a few looked over by hand for the mechanics (tool ordering, the queued outcome turn, the profile writes are app behaviour and the unit tests cover them): three per path, host failure, host success against a local listener that answers /server/info, and Bambu with the in-process fake. The 10-run measured batch only for question 1's reply wording.

Finding 03 in the report (version 7) matches this.

0a4d56a797122f5072d9a1d27a6514c5e1bbb932
Mark an added printer in the chat and always offer to connect it

After the printer assistant saved a printer, nothing in the thread marked
it, and what came next was the model's to improvise: measured over 30-run
samples, it offered to connect in 27-77% of replies after an add, and its
choices were mostly a bare "Yes | No".

- A "Printer added" card. PrinterConversation::add records a display-only
  block (kind "added": the saved printer's name and nozzle) under the
  message that added it, only when the save succeeds; the page draws it as
  a check, "Printer added", and "name · 0.4 mm nozzle", in design tokens.
  It never reaches the model. A refused or repeated add draws none. The
  name wraps rather than clipping, so a long one never hides the nozzle.
- The offer, spelled out. The printer prompt now ends the reply to a
  successful printer_add with exactly "Want to connect it so you can send
  prints straight to it?" and "Choices: Connect it | Not now". The model
  may still restate what the card says; that is fine.
- tests/printer_prompt: run_prompt_tests.py sends the model the requests
  the printer panel sends (the prompt rendered from printerInstructions.ts,
  the app's tool list, history with each earlier message's tool calls and
  results replayed as 115e2776bf does), answers the tools as the app does,
  and counts outcomes over many runs in seconds, without the app. Cases:
  connect a Bambu printer; name a model; choose one of three, on an Add
  session and tool answers recorded from a live run (add_session.json, the
  full 383-printer list). An agent_bridge_tests case fails when
  printer_tools.json drifts from the registry (JUSPRIN_UPDATE_PRINTER_TOOLS=1
  rewrites it). With the new line, each case passed 30 of 30.
- --printer-live checks that each add draws exactly one receipt under a
  message of the thread, that a second yes draws none, and, in a new step,
  that choosing "Prusa MK4S" from three draws one. With
  PRINTER_LIVE_CAPTURE_DIR set it writes a PNG of the panel at each of
  those points through WebKit's own snapshot (capture_panel).

Verified on macOS RelWithDebInfo: agent_bridge_tests 256 cases, AgentUI
Vitest 196, the prompt test 30 of 30 per case, and --printer-live passing
in light and dark with the real model, pictures reviewed.

649d74bca8a865dea145dfa9eae24be673df6e09
Refuse printer_connect calls that have nothing to connect to

When someone asked to connect a Moonraker or OctoPrint printer before
giving its address, the model sometimes called printer_connect with no
address ({"hostType":"moonraker"} or {"address":""}). The printer
panel's own check refused the call, but a refused call still becomes an
activity, and the panel draws every finished printer_connect activity as
"Connect this printer · Sent". The person saw a claim that something was
sent, and only then was asked for the address.

The registry's decoder now accepts exactly one of two argument sets: a
non-empty deviceId alone (Bambu Lab), or hostType with a non-empty
address (Moonraker or OctoPrint). A call the decoder refuses goes back
to the model as an error and never becomes an activity, so nothing is
drawn. The refusal and the schema descriptions tell the model to ask
for the address instead. The panel's check keeps only what the decoder
cannot know: a deviceId sent for a printer that is not a Bambu Lab one.

Verified live with the shell harness and the real model, typing as a
new user, with every call's arguments recorded through a local proxy:
before the change the false "Sent" block appeared in 2 of 3
conversations; after it, 0 of 4, including 2 where the model made the
same incomplete call and then asked for the address. Giving an address
still shows the credential card. agent_bridge_tests: 248 test cases
pass; the new test fails on the old decoder.

Not covered: other refusals from the panel's check (a wrong kind of
device id, an unsupported connection type) are still drawn as "Sent",
and an address that is really a printer name is still accepted.

c922876c66efb06bb862f527b00a33eeea8085e1
Keep the app responsive while it tests a printer's network address

Connecting a Moonraker or OctoPrint printer from the printer setup
conversation froze the whole app for as long as the printer took to
answer. OrcaPrinterBackend::connect_host ran Orca's blocking
PrintHost::test on the main thread, and a host that accepts the
connection but never replies holds that call with no upper bound
(Http's DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MAX is 0). Meanwhile the connect card said only
"Sent", nothing typed could land, and a failure ended in a reply with
no way forward. It also saved the address to the printer before
testing it, so Home said "Sends files over Wi-Fi" after a failed test.

Now:
- connect_host tests a copy of the printer's settings on a detached
  thread and returns at once. The thread owns the adapter and a verdict
  slot; the backend reads the verdict on the next connection() call.
  Nothing joins the thread, so closing the panel never waits on a slow
  host. The address and API key are saved only when the test passes.
- Host attempts share the Bambu path's 30-second limit
  (kConnectionWait), so a silent host is reported as failed at 30 s.
- A new printer_connect while one is waiting replaces it instead of
  being refused with connection_in_progress. The card's Cancel
  (printer_action cancel_connection) and the start of a new panel
  session drop a waiting attempt, and whatever the printer answers
  later is never read or saved.
- The conversation keeps each card's attempt state and sends it to the
  page, so the card reads Connecting… (with a progress bar and Cancel),
  then Connected, "Couldn't reach <address>" or Cancelled.
- printer_connect's result tells the model the wait ("gives it up to 30
  seconds"). The app sends only message text between turns, so the
  prompt asks the model to say the wait in its "checking" line, where a
  later question can find it. After a failure the prompt asks for the
  three ways forward in words: try again, enter the details in the
  printer settings, or leave it for now since the printer can prepare
  prints without a connection.

Not changed: a failed or cancelled Bambu Lab attempt still leaves the
printer linked to the device and selected. Undoing that is separate
work.

Verified:
- Shell harness (--printer-setup), unfixed build first: a host holding
  the request for 3 s froze a 100 ms timer for 3032 ms (0 ticks) and
  the failed address was saved. Fixed build: 29 ticks in 3010 ms,
  nothing saved; a silent host fails at 30.0 s while the timer keeps
  ticking; success saves the address; Cancel, a replaced attempt and a
  panel closed mid-test save nothing. The panel-close check was shown to
  fail with PrinterConversation::start()'s drop removed.
- agent_bridge_tests: 252 test cases pass, including new ones for
  connecting, replacing, cancelling, the dropped late answer, and a
  message sent while waiting being answered before the outcome's turn.
- AgentUI vitest: 193 tests pass, including the card's states.
- Live model, prompt-only runs (20 each): the failure reply names all
  three ways forward in 20/20 (17/20 also say the printer can still
  prepare prints); "skip it" 20/20; the wait is given as 30 s 20/20.
  An earlier wording ("enter the details themselves") dropped the
  unrelated "show me the full printer list" step from 85/90 to 66/90
  with the real catalogue in context; the committed wording is 29/30.
- Live app (--printer-live, 9 runs): the question typed while waiting
==================
115e2776bfd8852e10874510a297c841c77bacf6
Replay each chat's earlier tool calls and results to the model

Between turns the app sent the model only the text of earlier messages.
That lost what a tool had found: in the printer chat, after
printer_connection_status listed the printer's id in one turn, "connect
it" in the next turn had no id to use, and the model invented one, sent a
Moonraker host type for a Bambu printer, or looked the printer up again.

Every session now replays each earlier assistant message's tool calls
with their results, in the order made, in every chat: keeping the whole
transcript is what the model expects, and trimming is done selectively.
Each call and its result travel as one history entry, so the 20-entry
cap can never send a call without its output. A result over 16 KiB is
replayed as its state and a note to call the tool again. The workspace
that rides along with a project tool's live result is left out on
replay, since the turn carries the current one. The provider's call id
is saved with the activity (callId) so the replay uses the real one. The
OpenAI adapter emits function_call and function_call_output with that id
and without the item id, which with store:false names nothing the
service kept.

Measured against the shipped model with the printer session's real tools
and prompt, 5 runs each: text-only history connected correctly 0 of 5
times; with the replay, 5 of 5 called printer_connect with the listed
deviceId. The project chat was not measured live.

The printer prompt test on claude/printer-receipt-card still copies
text-only history and needs the same replay when the branches meet.

Screen Recording permission on macOS: screencapture and the harness's
screen blit get nothing there. The mode is macOS-only for that reason.

content.text:
All three are addressed on `jusprin-newui` as of commit 0a4d56a797 (today 11:13), with two small leftovers. I checked the code, not just the commit messages, and ran the Agent page tests locally (196 pass). The C++ and live-model counts below come from the commit messages; the test binary in this build directory predates the commits, so I did not rerun those.

**01, after-add moment left to the model: addressed** by 0a4d56a797. A successful `printer_add` now records a display-only "Printer added" block (name and nozzle) that the page draws under the message, and the prompt pins the offer word for word: "Want to connect it so you can send prints straight to it?" followed by "Choices: Connect it | Not now". A new prompt test harness under tests/printer_prompt reports 30 of 30 on each case. One open point: this offer still uses reply buttons. Your "no chips" call yesterday was made on the failure reply; I asked in the thread whether it also applies here and got no answer, so finding 01 in the report still describes buttons.

**02, connect card before an address exists: addressed** by 649d74bca8, the way the thread settled it. The registry decoder now accepts exactly one of two argument sets, a non-empty device id alone or a host type with a non-empty address, and a refused call goes back to the model as an error without becoming an activity, so no card is drawn. The schema descriptions and the refusal text tell the model to ask for the address first. Live before/after: the false card appeared in 2 of 3 conversations, then 0 of 4. Leftover, stated in the commit itself: an address that is really a printer name ("Creality K1") is still accepted, because only emptiness is checked, not shape.

**03, thirty seconds of silence: addressed** by c922876c66, covering all five pieces from the thread. The host test runs on a detached thread that owns the adapter and a verdict slot, with the same 30-second limit as the Bambu path. The card reads Connecting… with a progress bar and Cancel, then Connected, "Couldn't reach <address>", or Cancelled; the "Sent" label is gone. A new connect replaces a waiting one instead of being refused, and the panel's Cancel drops it. The tool result says "gives it up to 30 seconds". The prompt asks for the three ways forward in words with no Choices line, measured 20 of 20 live. The harness shows the bug first (a 100 ms timer stopped for 3 s) and the fix (29 ticks in 3 s).

**Bonus:** the address and key are now saved only when the test passes, which closes the Moonraker/OctoPrint half of finding 04. The Bambu half, where a failed or cancelled attempt leaves the device linked and selected, is explicitly left as separate work.

Supporting commits: 115e2776bf replays earlier tool calls and results to the model, which fixed the model inventing a device id on the next turn, and c013c97942 adds a harness mode that captures the connect flow's card states as PNGs through WebKit's own snapshot.
